title: Surender Singh Kasana vs Bhoodev Singh on 19 December, 2025
full_text: Surender Singh Kasana vs Bhoodev Singh on 19 December, 2025 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh IN THE COURT OF JUDICIAL MAGISTRATE FIRST CLASS (NI ACT-02), SOUTH EAST DISTRICT, SAKET COURT COMPLEX, NEW DELHI (Presided over by Ms. Shruti Sharma-I) DLSE020002492010 Criminal Complaint No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana ....................... Complainant Vs. Bhoodev Singh .......................Accused Sr.No Particulars Details A. Name and address of Shri Bhoodev Singh the Accused. S/o Shri Malkhan Singh R/o A-5B/132B, Janakpuri, New Delhi - 110058 (Note: Accused claims shifted to 3633, Sec. 23, Gurgaon, Haryana post sale of Janakpuri property on 08.07.2008; same address furnished in bail bond dated 28.05.2012). Page no.1/21 Digitally signed SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:53:56 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh JUDGMENT 1. This Court, by the present detailed judgment, adjudicates the complaint instituted by Surender Kasana (hereinafter "Complainant"). The complaint targets Sh. Bhoodev Singh (Accused), for offences punishable under Section 138 r/w Section 142 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (" NI Act "). The prosecution stems from the dishonour of one cheque allegedly issued by the Accused in purported discharge of a legally enforceable debt: Cheque No. 287244 dated 26.04.2010 for Rs. 6,00,000/- drawn on Citi Bank, Delhi. This cheque, handed over as payment of a liability from sale of car make Honda Accord was presented for encashment Syndicate Bank, Chattarpur Branch, but returned unpaid on 24.09.2010 with the bank endorsement "Account Closed". Despite statutory legal demand notice and the Accused's failure to remit payment within the prescribed 15-day window, the cause of action crystallized, warranting invocation of NI Act 's penal provisions. 2. The complainant, Sh. Surender Singh Kasana, states by way of present complaint that he is a law-abiding citizen and had cordial and long-standing relations with the accused, Sh. Bhoodev Singh. It is averred that the complainant was the owner of a Honda Accord car bearing registration no. DL-3C-AA-4316, which was financed through ICICI Bank. According to the complainant, in view of the friendly relations, the accused induced him to hand over the said car to him for a total consideration of ₹6,00,000/-. The accused further assured that he wou ld regularly pay the pending installments of the car loan to ICICI Bank on behalf of the complainant and would thereafter obtain and hand over the NOC to the complainant. Relying upon the said assurances, the complainant delivered possession of the vehicle to the accused. In discharge of his legal liability towards the agreed consideration amount, the accused issued cheque bearing no. 287244 dated 26.04.2010 for a sum of ₹6,00,000/- drawn on Citi Bank N.A., New Delhi, in favour of the complainant, and assured its encashment. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.19 Page no.2/21 16:53:58 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh 3. To the Complainant's profound dismay, the cheque was dishonoured upon presentment, evincing account closed--a fact corroborated by original return memo. Preceding assurances from the Accused notwithstanding, post-dishonour communications yielded only temporizing excuses and hollow pledges of imminent settlement. This pattern of evasion underscored a lack of genuine intent to honour the instruments. 4. Adhering scrupulously to Section 138 NI Act, the Complainant's counsel dispatched a comprehensive legal demand notice dated 20.10.2010 via speed post to the Accused's declared address. The notice categorically demanded repayment of the cheque amount within 15 days of receipt. Postal receipts confirm dispatch, with deemed service thereafter. The Accused's resounding silence--no payment, no rebuttal--fortified the presumption of liability under Section 139 NI Act. 5. The complainant contends that the deliberate issuance of cheque, their dishonour for account closed, and defiant non-compliance post-notice collectively constitute wilful default. This sequence repudiates any defence of bona fides, portraying calculated circumvention of a proven commercial obligation, squarely indictable under Section 138 NI Act. The complainant further contends that the Complainant's unimpugned averments and documents establish the foundational ingredients: a cheque issued in debt discharge, dishonour for account closed, and failed notice redressal. 6. Upon a careful perusal of the material placed on record along with the complaint, and after due examination of the complainant by way of pre-summoning evidence in accordance with the mandate of Section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, this Court was satisfied that a prima facie case was made out against the accused for the commission of an offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The evidence adduced at the pre-summoning stage Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.3/21 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:00 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh sufficiently disclosed the existence of a legally enforceable liability and the issuance of the cheque in question by the accused towards its discharge, followed by its dishonour due to account closed. Accordingly, vide order dated 10.05.2011, this Court was pleased to take cognizance of the offence and summoned the accused to face trial for the alleged dishonour of cheque issued in discharge of a debt or liability, as contemplated under the statutory scheme of the NI Act . 7. The accused appeared on 28.05.2012 with his counsel, and was granted bail by this Court on the very same date. Pursuant to the grant of bail, the accused was directed to furnish requisite bail bonds, and accordingly, he had furnished his bail bonds which were accepted. Subsequently, upon satisfaction that a prima facie case existed warranting trial, this Court proceeded to frame notice under Section 251 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 ( CrPC ), which was duly served upon the accused on 01.07.2014. Upon being apprised of the substance of accusation, including the specific allegations pertaining to issuance and dishonour of the cheque in question, the accused pleaded not guilty and claimed trial, thereby necessitating the recording of evidence in the matter in accordance with law. 8. Thereafter, in support of his case, the complainant adopted his pre-summoning evidence and tendered his evidence affidavit. Further more, the complainant examined two witnesses as CW-1 and CW-2 respectively. CW1/complainant entered the witness box and relied on the following documents in support of his case:- Sr. No. Exhibits Particulars 1. Ex.CW-1/A Original cheque bearing No. 287244 dated 26.04.2010 for a sum of ₹6,00,000/- drawn on Citi Bank N.A., New Delhi, allegedly issued by the accused in discharge of his legal liability. 2. Ex.CW-1/B Bank return memo dated 24.09.2010, whereby the cheque in question was returned unpaid with the Digitally signed Page no.4/21 SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:02 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh remarks "Account Closed". 3. Ex.CW-1/C Copy of legal demand notice dated 20.10.2010 sent by the complainant to the accused calling upon him to make payment of the cheque amount within the statutory period. 4. Ex.CW-1/D Postal receipt evidencing dispatch of the aforesaid legal notice through registered post. 5. Ex.CW-1/E UPC receipt evidencing dispatch of the legal notice through UPC. 6. Ex.CW-1/F The complaint filed by the complainant under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 7. Ex.CW-1/G Evidence Affidavit of complainant dated 01.12.2010. 9. The aforesaid stage was thereafter followed by an extensive examination-in-chief of CW-1, who was subjected to a detailed and searching cross-examination on behalf of the accused. Upon completion of such cross-examination, and no further questions remaining to be put to the witness by either side, CW-1 was formally discharged by the Court on 09.08.2016, in accordance with law. 10. CW-2/Sh. Mahesh Shukla, Area Debt Manager, ICICI Bank was examined in chief. He relied on the documents ie. Ex.CW-2/A self attested statement of loan account of the complainant. He was cross examined at length and was discharged on 18.09.2018. 11. Upon completion of the complainant evidence and as the complainant did not wish to examine any other witness, hence the matter fixed for recording of statement of accused u/s 313 CrPC and subsequent to the conclusion of the complainant's evidence, and in compliance with the procedural mandate under Section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, the statement of the accused was recorded by the Court on 03.10.2016 and subsequently an additional statement of the accused Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.5/21 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:04 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh u/s 313 CrPC was recorded on 11.02.2019, thereby affording him an opportunity to personally explain the incriminating circumstances appearing against him in the prosecution evidence. 12. Thereafter, the accused was afforded a full and fair opportunity to lead evidence in defence. The accused examined three witnesses in support of his case. DW-1/Sh. Jagdish Salwan, Manager, Citi Bank was examined in chief, cross examined and discharged on 24.10.2017. He had produced the account opening form of Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd. which is Ex.DW-1/A. DW-2/ Sh. R.K. Pahwa, Assistant Section Officer, Sheik Sarai Authority, South Zone was examined, cross examined and discharged on 20.11.2017. He had produced the record of the owners of the vehicle in question and relied on Ex.DW-2/A till Ex.DW-2/K. DW-3/ Sh. Narender Kumar, Civil Defense Volunteer, Office of Sub-Registrar-II, Basai, Darapur, Delhi was examined, cross examined and discharged on 02.04.2019. He has relied on the sale deed dated 08.07.2008 which is Ex.DW-3/1. 13. Consequently, vide separate statement recorded, DE was closed on 02.04.2019 and the matter was accordingly directed to proceed to the stage of final arguments. Final Arguments 14. Thereafter, this Court heard and considered the final arguments advanced on behalf of both the parties on 07.11.2025. Upon conclusion of the said submissions, the matter was reserved for pronouncement of judgment. 15. Learned counsel for the complainant submitted that the accused issued cheque bearing no. 287244 dated 26.04.2010 for a sum of ₹6,00,000/- drawn on Citi Bank N.A., New Delhi, in favour of the complainant towards discharge of his legal liability arising out of the sale of a Honda Accord car bearing registration no. DL-3C-AA-4316, possession whereof had already been taken by the accused. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 Page no.6/21 16:54:05 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh 16. It was argued that upon presentation, the said cheque was dishonoured vide return memo dated 24.09.2010 with the remarks "Account Closed", thereby clearly attracting the rigours of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. It was further submitted that a statutory legal demand notice was duly sent to the accused within the prescribed period, and despite service, the accused failed to make payment of the cheque amount within the statutory time. 17. Learned counsel contended that on the basis of pre-summoning evidence and the documents exhibited by the complainant, cognizance was taken and the accused was summoned to face trial. At the stage of notice under Section 251 CrPC, the accused did not deny his signatures on the cheque but took a vague defence that the cheque had been procured illegally, while also admitting that the address mentioned in the notice was the same as that furnished by him in his bail bond. 18. It was argued that the complainant duly proved the cheque in question (Ex. CW1/A), return memo (Ex. CW1/B), legal notice (Ex. CW1/C), postal receipt (Ex. CW1/D) and UPC receipt (Ex. CW1/E), and his testimony remained unimpeached in cross-examination. It was submitted that the accused failed to examine himself in defence and did not lead any cogent evidence to rebut the statutory presumptions under Sections 118(a) and 139 of the NI Act. 19. Learned counsel further submitted that the defence of non-receipt of legal notice is liable to be rejected in view of the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in C.C. Alavi Haji v. Palapetty Muhammed &Anr. , (2007) 6 SCC 555 , as the notice was sent to the correct address of the accused and, even otherwise, no payment was made despite receipt of summons from the Court. Reliance was also placed on Kalu Ram v. Sita Ram , 1980 RLR (Note) 44 and L.C. Goyal v. Suresh Joshi, to contend that failure to reply to the legal notice raises an adverse inference against the accused. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.19 16:54:07 Page no.7/21 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh 20. It was also argued that though the accused claimed in his statement under Section 313 CrPC that he had no connection with the account on which the cheque was drawn, the bank witness (DW-1) proved that the account of M/s Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd. was operated by the accused as one of its authorised signatories, thereby falsifying his defence. 21. Learned counsel emphasized that in view of the authoritative pronouncements of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee , ( 2001) 6 SCC 16, Rangappa v. Sri Mohan , ( 2010) 11 SCC 441 andBasalingappa v. Mudibasappa , (2019) 5 SCC 418, once the execution of the cheque is admitted, a presumption arises regarding existence of a legally enforceable debt, and the burden lies upon the accused to rebut the same on a preponderance of probabilities, which burden has not been discharged in the present case. 22. It was finally contended that the accused neither replied to the statutory notice nor made any payment even after appearance before the Court, and has taken false and inconsistent pleas only to evade liability, thereby demonstrating his dishonest conduct. Hence, all the ingredients of Section 138 of the NI Act stand proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused deserves to be convicted. 23. Learned counsel for the accused submitted that the present complaint is liable to be dismissed as the essential ingredients of Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 are not fulfilled. 24. It was argued that no Honda Accord car bearing registration no. DL-3CAA-4316 was ever sold or handed over by the complainant to the accused, and that there was no transaction of sale or any legally enforceable debt or liability between the parties. It was contended that the complainant failed to produce any documentary proof of ownership, sale, delivery, or transfer of the vehicle, nor any receipt evidencing handing over of possession, and even in cross-examination admitted absence of such documents. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 Page no.8/21 16:54:09 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh 25. Learned counsel further submitted that the cheque in question does not belong to the accused in his individual capacity but was drawn on the account of M/s Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd., which, as per DW-1 (Bank Manager, Citi Bank), stood closed on 12.05.2009. It was argued that since the company was neither impleaded as an accused nor were the requirements of Section 141 NI Act satisfied, the prosecution against the accused in his personal capacity is not maintainable, reliance being placed on AneetaHada v. Godfather Travels & Tours (P) Ltd., (2012) 5 SCC 661. 26. It was also contended that the accused is not the "drawer" of the cheque within the meaning of Section 138 NI Act and therefore cannot be fastened with criminal liability, particularly when the cheque pertains to a company account and the alleged transaction is claimed to be personal. 27. With regard to service of legal demand notice, it was argued that the statutory notice dated 20.10.2010 was never served upon the accused, as he had already sold the property bearing no. A-5B/132B, Janakpuri, New Delhi on 08.07.2008, much prior to issuance of the notice. In support, reliance was placed on the testimony of DW-3 from the office of Sub-Registrar and the sale deed. It was submitted that service of notice being a mandatory requirement under proviso (b) to Section 138 NI Act, non-service vitiates the complaint. Reliance was placed on Jugesh Sehgal v. Shamsher Singh Gogi , ( 2009) 14 SCC 683, M.D. Thomas v. P.S. Jaleel , (2009) 14 SCC 398, and other authorities to contend that deemed service cannot be presumed when the accused was not residing at the said address. 28. Learned counsel further argued that DW-2 from the RTO proved that the vehicle in question was never purchased by the accused and, as per official records, was sold by the complainant to one Sunil Kumar on 06.10.2010 and thereafter to Rakesh Kumar, thereby demolishing the complainant's case that the accused had purchased or possessed the car. Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 Page no.9/21 16:54:11 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh 29. It was submitted that in view of the aforesaid defence evidence, the accused has successfully rebutted the statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act by raising a probable defence, and that the complainant has failed to establish the existence of any legally enforceable debt or liability. Reliance was placed on Krishna Janardhan Bhat v. Dattatraya G. Hegde , AIR 2008 SC 1325, to contend that presumption stands rebutted once a probable defence is shown. 30. It was further argued that the complainant failed to prove that he was a holder in due course of the cheque and that the cheque was not obtained through lawful means, particularly when no liability of the accused stood established and the cheque allegedly pertained to a third-party company. 31. Learned counsel emphasized that the accused has discharged his burden on the standard of preponderance of probabilities, while the complainant has failed to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt, as required in criminal jurisprudence. Reliance was also placed on recent authority in Rajaram v. Maruthachalam (2023) to reiterate the presumption of innocence and the standard of proof. On these grounds, it was prayed that the accused be acquitted and the complaint be dismissed. Legal Analysis & Findings:- 32. I have heard at considerable length the detailed arguments advanced by the learned counsel appearing for the complainant as well as the learned counsel representing the accused. Their respective submissions have been carefully analyzed in the context of the factual matrix and the legal principles applicable to the case. This Court has also undertaken a thorough and meticulous scrutiny of the entire judicial record, which includes the contents of the complaint, the affidavits and supporting documents annexed thereto, the oral testimonies of the complainant's and the defence witnesses, if any, recorded during the course of trial, and all exhibits relied upon by the respective parties. Each piece of evidence has been examined Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA SHRUTI Date: Page no.10/21 SHARMA 2025.12.19 16:54:12 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh individually as well as in conjunction with the other evidence on record so as to assess its evidentiary value, credibility, and probative strength. The rival submissions have been objectively evaluated against the backdrop of the statutory framework and the well-settled legal position governing proceedings under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The Court has, therefore, endeavored to reach a reasoned and just determination by adopting a holistic and balanced appreciation of the evidence and circumstances presented before it. 33. Before embarking upon a discussion on the merits of the present case, it is considered apposite to first delineate the legal framework governing the offence of dishonour of cheque, as encapsulated under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The legislative intent behind enacting Section 138 is to instill greater financial discipline and sanctity in contractual obligations by deterring the issuance of cheque without sufficient funds or without adequate arrangements with the banker. The provision prescribes penal consequences in the event of dishonor of a cheque on grounds of insufficiency of funds or if the amount exceeds the arrangement with the bank, thereby recognizing the cheque as a legitimate instrument of payment in the eyes of the law. 34. In order to fasten criminal liability upon an accused under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, it is incumbent upon the complainant to plead and prove the existence of certain foundational ingredients through the averments made in the complaint and the evidence led during the course of trial. The essential ingredients that must be cumulatively satisfied are as follows: a.That the accused must have drawn a cheque on an account maintained by him with a banker, for the payment of a certain sum of money to another person, and such payment must have been intended for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a legally enforceable debt or other liability; Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 Page no.11/21 16:54:14 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh b.That the said cheque must have been presented to the bank within a period of three months from the date on which it was drawn, or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier; c.That upon such presentation, the cheque must have been returned unpaid by the bank, either due to insufficiency of funds in the drawer's account or because the amount exceeded the arrangement made by the drawer with the bank; d.That the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque must have issued a written statutory demand notice to the drawer, seeking payment of the cheque amount, within 30 days from the date of receipt of information from the bank regarding the return of the cheque unpaid; e.That the drawer of the cheque, despite the receipt of such legal notice, failed to make payment of the cheque amount to the payee or holder in due course within 15 days from the date of such receipt. 35. Only upon proof of the aforementioned ingredients does the offence under Section 138 stand attracted, subject to the operation of statutory presumptions under Sections 118 and 139 of the NI Act. These presumptions, however, are rebuttable and impose a reverse burden upon the accused to dislodge the same on a preponderance of probabilities. 36. It is also pertinent to note that, as per the Explanation appended to Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, the expression "debt or other liability" refers exclusively to a legally enforceable debt or other liability. This legal clarification is of critical significance, as it makes clear that mere issuance of a cheque is not sufficient to attract penal liability under the statute. The dishonouredcheque must have been issued in discharge of a debt or liability which is subsisting and legally enforceable at the time of its issuance. A cheque issued as a gift, donation, or Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.12/21 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:16 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh towards a time-barred or non-existent liability will not fall within the purview of Section 138 . Thus, the complainant must establish that at the time the cheque was drawn, there existed a valid and enforceable obligation in law for which the cheque was issued. 37. It is well-settled in law that the aforementioned ingredients must co-exist and be satisfied cumulatively in order to constitute the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. The absence or non-fulfilment of even one of these statutory requirements is fatal to the prosecution's case and would disentitle the complainant from invoking penal liability against the drawer of the cheque. 38. After hearing the rival contentions from both the parties and perusal of judicial record, it is revealed that the gravamen of the controversy is whether any person who has been mentioned in Sections 141(1) and 141(2) of the Act can be prosecuted without the company being impleaded as an accused. To appreciate the controversy, certain provisions need to be referred to. Section 138 of the Act, which deals with the ingredients of the offence for dishonour of the cheque and the consequent non-payment of the amount due thereon, reads as follows: - "138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc, of funds in the account - Where any cheque drawn by a person on account maintained by him with a banker for the payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an arrangement made with the bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with Digitally signed by SHRUTI SHARMA Page no.13/21 SHRUTI Date: SHARMA 2025.12.19 16:54:18 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh imprisonment for a term which may be extended to two years, or with a fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless - (a) the cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier, (b) the payee or the holder in due course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer of the cheque, within thirty days of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheque as unpaid, and (c) the drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice." 39. The main part of the provision can be segregated into three compartments, namely, (i) the cheque is drawn by a person, (ii) the cheque drawn on an account maintained by him with the banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of a debt or other liability, is returned unpaid, either because the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an arrangement made with the bank and (iii) such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall, without prejudice to any other provision of the Act, be punished with imprisonment for a term which may extend to two years or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque or with both. The proviso to the said section postulates under what circumstances the section shall not apply. In the case at hand, we are not concerned with the said aspect. It will not be out of place to Digitally signed Page no.14/21 SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:20 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh state that the main part of the provision deals with the basic ingredients and the proviso deals with certain circumstances and lays certain conditions where it will not be applicable. The emphasis has been laid on the factum that the cheque has to be drawn by a person on the account maintained by him and he must have issued the cheque in discharge of any debt or other liability. Section 7 of the Act defines 'drawer' to mean the maker of a bill of exchange or a cheque. An authorised signatory of a company becomes a drawer as he has been authorised to do so in respect of the account maintained by the company. 40. At this juncture, we may refer to Section 141 which deals with offences by companies. As the spine of the controversy rests on the said provision, it is reproduced below: - "141. Offences by companies. - (1) If the person committing an offence under section 138 is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of, and was responsible to the company for the conduct of the business of the company, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly; Provided that nothing contained in this sub-section shall render any person liable to punishment if he proves that the offence was committed without his knowledge, or that he had exercised all due diligence to prevent the commission of such offence: Provided further that where a person is nominated as a Director of a Company by virtue of his holding any office or employment in the Central Government or State Government or a financial corporation owned or controlled by the Central Government or the State Government, as the case may be, he shall not be liable for prosecution Digitally signed by under this Chapter. SHRUTI SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: Page no.15/21 2025.12.19 16:54:22 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh (2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1), where any offence under this Act, has been committed by a company and it is proved that the offence has been committed with the consent or connivance of, or is attributable to, any neglect on the part of, any director, manager, secretary or other officer of the company, such director, manager, secretary or other officer shall also be deemed to be guilty of that offence and shall be liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly." 41. On a reading of the said provision, it is plain as day that if a person who commits offence under Section 138 of the Act is a company, the company as well as every person in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of business of the company at the time of commission of offence is deemed to be guilty of the offence. The first proviso carves out under what circumstances the criminal liability would not be fastened. Sub-section (2) enlarges the criminal liability by incorporating the concepts of connivance, negligence and consent that engulfs many categories of officers. It is worth noting that in both the provisions, there is a 'deemed' concept of criminal liability. 42. The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the landmark Constitution Bench decision Aneeta Hada v. Godfather Travels & Tours (P) Ltd. , (2012) 5 SCC 661 has settled the law authoritatively and held that the position that emerges can be summarised thus: (i) The prosecution of a person in charge of, and responsible to, the company for the conduct of the business of the company may not, in certain circumstances, be deemed to be sufficient. (ii) The company ought to be arraigned as an accused and be present before the court. (iii) It would be necessary to specifically aver in the complaint that the person accused was in charge of, or responsible for, the conduct of the business of the company. (iv) If the accused, being a director in the company, is not in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of the Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.16/21 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:25 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh business of the company, he is not liable. (v) The compliance of the above aspects would be a condition precedent to attract the vicarious liability as provided under Section 141 of the Act. It was further held that The legislature has incorporated the deeming fiction under Section 141 of the Act. When a statute enacts that something shall be deemed to have been done, which in fact and truth was not done, the court is entitled and bound to ascertain for what purposes and between what persons the statutory fiction is to be resorted to. There is no scope for drawing any inference beyond it. The fiction has to stop where it was intended to stop. 43. In SMS Pharmaceuticals Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla , (2005) 8 SCC 89, it was held that Criminal liability is attracted only on the drawer of the cheque who has failed to make the payment of the cheque amount despite receipt of a notice of demand. Liability is made more stringent by virtue of the fact that the cheque is drawn on a bank account maintained by the drawer. While the liability of the drawer of the cheque remains unaltered irrespective of whether the cheque is drawn on a personal or company bank account, the liability of persons in charge of the company arises only when the conditions specified in Section 141 are satisfied. 44. The cheque in question, bearing No. 287244 dated 26.04.2010 for a sum of ₹6,00,000/-, drawn on Citibank N.A., Account No. 0802472226, conspicuously bears the endorsement "For Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd." under the signature of the authorised signatory, as is evident from Ex. CW-1/A. DW-1, Mr. Jagdish Salwan, Manager, Citibank, has categorically deposed that the said account belonged exclusively to Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd. and that the same stood closed on 12.05.2009, as reflected from the account opening form Ex. DW-1/A. Despite this, the present prosecution has been instituted only against the accused in his individual capacity under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act. The company, namely Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd., which is the account holder and on whose behalf the cheque was drawn, has neither been impleaded as an accused Digitally signed Page no.17/21 SHRUTI by SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:27 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh nor are there any averments in the complaint Ex. CW-1/F or in the statutory legal notice Ex. CW-1/C invoking Section 141 of the NI Act so as to attribute vicarious liability to the accused. 45. Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 penalises the dishonour of a cheque "drawn by a person on an account maintained by him" for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any legally enforceable debt or liability. The expression "a person" undoubtedly includes both natural persons as well as juristic entities such as companies. However, where the drawer of the cheque is a company, Section 141(1) of the Act provides the sole statutory mechanism for fastening criminal liability. It mandates that "if the person committing an offence under Section 138 is a company, every person who, at the time the offence was committed, was in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business, as well as the company, shall be deemed to be guilty of the offence." The legislative scheme is thus unambiguous: in cases of corporate drawers, the company itself is the principal offender, and only thereafter can vicarious liability be fastened upon its officers or directors subject to the requisite pleadings and proof. The inevitable corollary is that non-impleadment of the company, which is the drawer and principal offender, strikes at the very root of the prosecution and constitutes a fundamental and incurable infirmity, rendering the proceedings against the officers or directors alone legally untenable. 46. The instant complaint squarely exemplifies this fatal vice. The complainant has neither arrayed the company, namely Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd., as an accused nor laid any foundational averments to invoke vicarious liability under Section 141 of the NI Act. On the contrary, the case set up in the complaint is of an alleged personal transaction, namely the sale/transfer of car bearing registration no. DL-3C-AA-4316 for a consideration of ₹6,00,000/-, while the cheque relied upon (Ex. CW1/A) is admittedly drawn on the bank account of the company and Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.18/21 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:29 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. Bhoodev Singh bears the endorsement "For Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd." By its authorised signatory. There is thus a clear mismatch between the alleged personal liability and the corporate instrument produced in evidence. Significantly, neither in the complaint nor in the statutory legal demand notice is there even a whisper that the accused, at the relevant time, was "in charge of and responsible to the company for the conduct of its business," as mandatorily required under Section 141(1) of the NI Act. Such basic pleadings being conspicuously absent, the prosecution against the accused in his individual capacity is legally unsustainable. It is now well settled by a catena of decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court and various High Courts that, in the absence of impleadment of the company as the principal offender and in the absence of specific averments satisfying the ingredients of Section 141 , directors or officers of the company cannot be prosecuted or convicted for an offence under Section 138 . The non- compliance in the present case goes to the root of the matter and is fatal to the maintainability of the complaint itself. 47. Independently of the aforesaid infirmity, the defence has demolished the substratum of case of the complainant regarding the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability under Section 139 of the NI Act. The RTO records brought on record through DW-2, and proved as Ex. DW2/A to Ex. DW2/K, unequivocally establish that the complainant had already transferred and sold the vehicle in question to one Sunil Kumar on 06.10.2010. This fact is of decisive significance, as it precedes the alleged subsisting liability sought to be enforced through the cheque in question, which was presented on 24.09.2010. Once the vehicle stood sold and ownership transferred, the very foundation of the complainant's plea of an outstanding consideration payable by the accused stood extinguished. Significantly, the complainant has failed to produce any sale agreement, delivery receipt, or contemporaneous document to show that the accused continued to be liable towards him after such transfer. Bhoodev Singh Bank loan records proved through CW-2 (Ex. CW2/A) do not reflect any subsisting liability of the accused corresponding to the alleged transaction and remain inconclusive and un-updated in this regard. 48. In the cumulative assessment of the evidence and the legal position discussed hereinabove, this Court is of the considered view that the very foundation of the prosecution under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act stands vitiated. Firstly, the cheque in question is not drawn by the accused in his individual capacity but is drawn on the account of Kuber Travels Pvt. Ltd., as is evident from the endorsement on the cheque itself and the testimony of DW-1. The accused, therefore, cannot be treated as the "drawer" of the cheque within the meaning of Section 138 NI Act. Secondly, despite the cheque being of a company account, the company has not been arrayed as an accused, nor does the complaint or the legal demand notice contain any averments satisfying the mandatory requirements of Section 141 NI Act so as to fasten vicarious liability upon the accused. In the absence of impleadment of the principal offender, namely the company, and in the absence of foundational pleadings that the accused was in charge of and responsible for the conduct of its business at the relevant time, the present prosecution against the accused in his individual capacity is legally not maintainable ab initio. Thirdly, even on merits, the complainant has failed to establish the existence of a legally enforceable debt or liability. On the contrary, the defence evidence, particularly the RTO records proved as Ex. DW2/A to Ex. DW2/K, probabilises that the alleged liability stood extinguished prior to the presentation of the cheque, thereby effectively rebutting the statutory presumption under Section 139 NI Act. Once such presumption stands rebutted, the burden reverted upon the complainant to prove the liability beyond reasonable doubt, which he has failed to discharge. 49. Thus, all the essential ingredients of Section 138 NI Act fail on a cumulative reading of the record: (i) the accused is not the drawer of the cheque; (ii) the Digitally signed by SHRUTI Page no.20/21 SHRUTI SHARMA SHARMA Date: 2025.12.19 16:54:33 +0530 Ct Case No. 616070/2016 Surender Singh Kasana Vs. The complaint, therefore, suffers from incurable legal infirmities and is not maintainable in the eyes of law. Conclusion 50. In the light of the aforementioned discussion, Accused Sh. Bhoodev Singh is hereby held not guilty and stands acquitted for the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881. 51.
